text: What last night showed us is that Americans are tired of being told that their needs are
unrealistic by politicians who have been bought by the wealthiest people in the country.
This country has elected a new generation of leadership, a generation with a mandate
to lower the cost of living, to build not bomb, to never betray the working people
who entrusted them with power.
And I hear often that the politics that we're fighting for here in New York City
are not possible outside of city limits.
And what last night showed us is that working people are the majority,
whether we are speaking of Austin or Ann Arbor or Astoria.
And it is time to put those same people first in our politics.
And last night shows us that it's possible to do so all across the country.
What specific things should Democrats do first?
For example, should one of their first acts be to vote to end the war in Iran?
I'm not saying that has to be your answer,
but I'm looking for that sort of specific action item you would suggest for Democrats.
Well, I appreciate this question because I think what it gets to, Henry,
is the fact that it is not enough for us as Democrats to win power.
We have to use that power to deliver change that Americans can feel in their wallets.
And to me, when you look at these campaigns,
if we want to speak about James Tallarico,
he campaigned on a vision for universal child care.
If you want to talk about Keisha Lance Bottoms,
she campaigned on a vision of cutting red tape to actually be able
to build housing at the speed that's needed.
If you want to talk about Jocelyn Benson,
she campaigned on a moratorium for data centers.
These, to me, are examples of the kind of specifics.
But again, what I'm excited to see now is a recognition that the work is only just starting
and that this has to be delivered for working people across the country.
Calling Abdul, did you call him out?
I haven't spoken to him yet.
I'm sure he is quite busy.
I've had the privilege of speaking to him in the past.
And I have to say that his election is one that means so much to so many.
And to see that victory in the face that all that he had to reckon with
over the course of that campaign,
whether in terms of the extraordinary amount of money spent to oppose him
or the racism and slander that he was met with on a daily basis,
it is incredibly exciting to see, as he said last night, that the good guys won.
What was it like watching the Blue Wave last night,
all the wins from New Yorkers, and so many firsts?
And also specifically, what is your plan that translates last night's
wins to helping everyday New Yorkers?
It was incredible to see the Blue Wave and to say words that I never thought
would be together in a sentence.
South Carolina, Kansas, Iowa, the races that are still yet to be called,
that these are even in question, it speaks to the fact that
this entire country is ready for a politics that means something
to their lives and to their struggles.
And what we saw Democrats running on across the country
was an ambition for what government could do,
as opposed to a sense that our job is simply to describe working people's struggles.
Our job is to deliver on those struggles.
And the commonality between working people in Austin and Ann Arbor in
Astoria across this country is one that should inspire also a commonality
of purpose for what we do with this power.
Because I see in that the true reflection of what the American people want,
which is change they can feel in their wallets.
It means that we can go from being on the defensive to being on the offensive.
The defensive means trying to prevent as many New Yorkers as possible
from losing their SNAP benefits or losing their health insurance.
That's a reflection of the policies that Republicans have pursued
for the last few years.
The offensive is delivering to make life more affordable for them.
That's what we've been focused on here in New York City,
and that's what we could do so much more of
if we had federal partners across the board,
and now we're seeing the election of many of them.
There's a lot of momentum in the...
Do you think that the left should continue to kind of press its foot down on the gas?
Or is there a risk of too much feuding,
factoring the party ahead of an important financial cycle?
Foot on the gas.
This is the moment where we are seeing people across this country
vote for a politics that will mean something.
For a long time politics has felt like a hobby only some people can afford.
We want politics to mean the deliverance of dignity into working people's lives
and to look at the victories.
Not just last night, but even in the primaries.
Going through yesterday evening.
It's a realization that it's a new dawn in America.
It's a new day in America.
And I cannot wait to see what we do with this opportunity
because it is one that we now must deliver on.
